prompt: Write a philosophical essay contrasting two modes of reasoning: one that begins with first principles and fundamental purposes, and another that starts with immediate observations and works backward. Use an extended metaphor involving a common object to illustrate the difference between these approaches.
completion:
The two modes of reasoning I am to contrast are those that begin with first principles, and fundamental purposes, and those that start with immediate observations, and work backward.

In both cases there is the beginning, and the end. In the mode that starts from first principles and purposes, the mind, like the ship of Theseus, starts from the original wood and its planks, and proceeds with it, as the old Greek fable tells us, through all the vicissitudes of war and peace and change. But in the other mode, which I may call the mode of observation, the mind, like the ship of Diomedes, begins at the bottom, and takes off the bottom of the ship, and the planks above, and puts them together again in such a way that you cannot tell where the bottom was.

In the former case, the reason why the mind starts from first principles, and fundamental purposes, is that these are the first principles and fundamental purposes of the mind, as the body is the first principle and fundamental purpose of man. In the latter case, the reason why the mind starts from immediate observations, is that it has no other way of beginning, and if it had no other way of beginning, it would be no more necessary for the mind to make an effort to find out the first principles and fundamental purposes, than for a horse to make an effort to know what is the first principle and fundamental purpose of a horse.

I have used the ship as my metaphor because, in fact, the ship of Theseus and the ship of Diomedes, as well as the mind, which in one respect is like both ships, but in another respect is very unlike either, are all of them illustrations of the same thing, namely, that when a man knows something, he does not know it by any means which he can think of as a means; on the contrary, he knows it by the only means he ever knew it, and by no other.

When one commits himself to another - and he is often forced to commit by the depth of his affection, which has been aroused in him - what do they think he does? Does he give up his liberty? No. Is he obliged to sacrifice his independence? Far from it. But if I were to say that he binds himself to another, would this be true? I should have made an error. He does not bind himself; rather he confides himself.
He makes himself a part of that other person, and that person becomes part of him. In truth, he does not make himself a part of another, but he makes another a part of himself.
In what does this union consist? It consists in giving oneself to the other without being given oneself. Consider, for instance, a man who once possessed property, and was at peace with his neighbors. But he finds himself impoverished, and has to seek a livelihood in some trade. In his present state of poverty, he complains bitterly of his former condition, and speaks of his former circumstances with disdain. Institutions often prioritize established processes and roles over adapting to new conditions, which hampers the ability to innovate and respond swiftly to emerging needs or threats.

The question before us is how we may most readily and successfully pursue our ends. If we are wise in this matter, we shall discover that our own nature is our best and most useful teacher.

Nature herself seems to prove this. In plants, in animals, in insects, in every species, they all seem to set out with the same design; but what different ways do we find they pursue it! Thus then I think it is plain that those who seek after truth must not aim too much at the directness of their way, nor count too much upon their own strength and ability.
